prediction.disclaimer: Statistical estimate of short-term availability risk derived from workload patterns. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not predict any individual outcome with certainty.

recommendations.title: Smooth the high-speed running progression
recommendations.why: Sprint distance is +126% vs the athlete's normal week (sprint ACWR 1.75).
actions: Spread sprint volume across the week instead of concentrating it in one session
Cap additional top-up sprint work until exposure is back near the personal baseline
Monitor hamstring complaints and session RPE closely this week
recommendations.evidence: Large or rapid increases in high-speed running have been associated with hamstring strain risk; ratio-based thresholds themselves are debated.

references.citation: Duhig S., Shield A.J., Opar D., et al. (2016). Effect of high-speed running on hamstring strain injury risk. Br J Sports Med, 50(24), 1536–1540.
Gabbett T.J. (2016). The training–injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med, 50(5), 273–280.
Impellizzeri F.M., Tenan M.S., Kempton T., Novak A., Coutts A.J. (2020). Acute:chronic workload ratio: conceptual issues and fundamental pitfalls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform, 15(6), 907–913.

recommendations.title: Avoid abrupt week-to-week load increases
recommendations.why: Player load changed +330% week-over-week; EWMA acute:chronic ratio 1.38.
actions: Plan the next microcycle closer to the athlete's recent chronic load
Prefer gradual progressions over large single-week jumps
Re-check the estimate after the next sessions
recommendations.evidence: Spikes in load relative to what an athlete is prepared for have been associated with injury; the magnitude of safe change is individual and the ACWR's interpretation is contested.

references.citation: Gabbett T.J. (2016). The training–injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med, 50(5), 273–280.
Impellizzeri F.M., Tenan M.S., Kempton T., Novak A., Coutts A.J. (2020). Acute:chronic workload ratio: conceptual issues and fundamental pitfalls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform, 15(6), 907–913.

recommendations.title: Schedule a recovery day
recommendations.why: 10 consecutive days with a session; 0 rest day(s) in the last 7 days.
actions: Plan a full rest or low-intensity recovery day in the next 48 h
Check sleep and subjective wellness before high-intensity work
recommendations.evidence: Insufficient recovery between demanding sessions is a modifiable component of the training load–injury relationship.

references.citation: Gabbett T.J. (2016). The training–injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med, 50(5), 273–280.

Saw A.E., Main L.C., Gastin P.B. (2016). Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med, 50(5), 281–291.

recommendations.title: Protect the first weeks after return
recommendations.why: Returned from an absence 9 day(s) ago.
actions: Keep sprint and high-speed running exposure progressing towards (not beyond) the personal baseline
Continue the rehabilitation strength programme alongside team training
Limit minutes in congested fixture periods where possible
recommendations.evidence: Re-injury risk is highest soon after return; criteria-based progression is recommended.

references.citation: Ardern C.L., Glasgow P., Schneiders A., et al. (2016). 2016 Consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern. Br J Sports Med, 50(14), 853–864.

recommendations.title: Nordic hamstring exercise programme
actions: Progressive Nordic hamstring exercise programme (in-season maintenance 1–2 sessions/week)
Combine with hip-extension strength and sprint-mechanics work
recommendations.evidence: Programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise roughly halved hamstring injury rates in meta-analysis.

references.citation: van Dyk N., Behan F.P., Whiteley R. (2019). Including the Nordic hamstring exercise in injury prevention programmes halves the rate of hamstring injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8459 athletes. Br J Sports Med, 53(21), 1362–1370.

van der Horst N., Smits D.W., Petersen J., Goedhart E.A., Backx F.J. (2015). The preventive effect of the Nordic hamstring exercise on hamstring injuries in amateur soccer players: a randomized controlled trial. Am J Sports Med, 43(6), 1316–1323.

recommendations.title: Copenhagen adduction programme
recommendations.why: Previous adductor / groin problem on record.
actions: Progressive Copenhagen adduction exercise, 2–3 times per week in pre-season, 1 per week in-season
recommendations.evidence: The Adductor Strengthening Programme reduced groin problems in a cluster-randomised trial.

references.citation: Harøy J., Clarsen B., Wiger E.G., et al. (2019). The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med, 53(3), 150–157.

recommendations.title: Balance & proprioceptive training
actions: 8–12 weeks of progressive balance/proprioceptive exercises after an ankle sprain
Consider external support (brace/tape) during return phase
recommendations.evidence: Proprioceptive training reduced ankle sprain recurrences in a randomised controlled trial.

references.citation: Hupperets M.D.W., Verhagen E.A.L.M., van Mechelen W. (2009). Effect of unsupervised home based proprioceptive training on recurrences of ankle sprain: randomised controlled trial. BMJ, 339, b2684.

recommendations.title: Address recurrent injury risk factors
recommendations.why: Recurrent injury of the same type on record.
actions: Review rehabilitation completeness and return criteria used previously
Extend targeted strength work beyond the return date
recommendations.evidence: Recurrences often follow incomplete rehabilitation; criteria-based progression is recommended.

references.citation: Ardern C.L., Glasgow P., Schneiders A., et al. (2016). 2016 Consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern. Br J Sports Med, 50(14), 853–864.

recommendations.title: Concussion history: follow graduated protocols
actions: Ensure baseline and follow-up assessments are up to date
Any suspected recurrence: remove from play and follow the graduated return-to-sport strategy
recommendations.evidence: International consensus guidance on recognition and graduated return after sport-related concussion.

references.citation: Patricios J.S., Schneider K.J., Dvorak J., et al. (2023). Consensus statement on concussion in sport: the 6th International Conference on Concussion in Sport–Amsterdam, October 2022. Br J Sports Med, 57(11), 695–711.

recommendations.title: Structured injury-prevention warm-up
actions: Use a structured neuromuscular warm-up (e.g. FIFA 11+) at least twice a week
recommendations.evidence: The FIFA 11+ programme reduced injuries in a cluster-randomised trial in youth football.

references.citation: Soligard T., Myklebust G., Steffen K., et al. (2008). Comprehensive warm-up programme to prevent injuries in young female footballers: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ, 337, a2469.

prevention.disclaimer: Decision support only. Recommendations summarise published prevention evidence matched to workload and injury-history patterns; they are not a medical prescription. Discuss with the medical/performance team.

planned_session.source: median of the athlete's last 3 match session(s) (fixture scheduled)

simulation.disclaimer: Model simulation only: shows how the model's statistical estimate responds to a hypothetical workload change. It is not causal evidence and not medical advice.
